abstract: De novo genes, arising from previously non coding regions, have defied our view of gene birth and proteome evolution. Advances in ribosome profiling and comparative genomics have uncovered widespread translation of de novo small open reading frames (sORFs), many of which encode previously unrecognized microproteins. Despite increasing evidence demonstrating translation of de novo sORFs, it remains poorly understood how their encoded microproteins acquire molecular functions. Here, we selected 30 de novo-emerged microproteins for structural characterization and investigated their potential for interacting with canonical protein domains. Using circular dichroism and small angle X-ray scattering we found that the studied young microproteins are disordered but may adopt helical conformations in specific contexts. Additionally, we identified predicted short linear motifs (SLiMs) recognized by canonical peptide-binding domains in 29 microprotein sequences, suggesting a potential for interaction with the conserved proteome. In vitro experimental validation revealed interactions with relevant affinities, with some on par with canonical interactions. We also show how a microprotein SLiM can easily evolve towards higher affinities for the binding partner. Together, our findings suggest that the intrinsically disordered de novo microproteins can exploit SLiM-mediated molecular recognition to engage the pre-existing proteome, providing a potential mechanism for their functional integration into cellular interaction networks.
